Girl Power
GURL POW-er
noun, phrase (Gen X slang)
From the riot grrrl punk scene of the early 1990s in Olympia, Washington, and Washington, D.C., where the band Bikini Kill and its photocopied zines used girl power as a rallying cry (c. 1991). The British pop group the Spice Girls took it worldwide in 1996–97 with their debut single "Wannabe" and a flood of interviews and merchandise; by 1997 girl power was printed on T-shirts and lunchboxes. The phrase names a cheerful, market-friendly feminism of female confidence, friendship, and independence.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Girl power was the slogan of the late 1990s: a lunchbox, a T-shirt, a Spice Girls chorus, and the message to a little girl that she could be strong, loud, and anything she wanted. Behind the merchandise was a real question every daughter asks: is there strength for me, and where does it come from? Scripture answers yes, and then answers better than the slogan. The Bible is full of strong women: Deborah, who arose "a mother in Israel" when the men faltered (Jdg 5:7); Esther, told she had come to the kingdom "for such a time as this" (Est 4:14); the virtuous woman who "girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms" (Pro 31:17), of whom it is said, "Strength and honour are her clothing" (Pro 31:25). But Scripture never locates the power in the girl. "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Deborah’s strength was God’s deliverance; Esther’s courage was obedience at the risk of her life. And the strongest thing Paul ever learned was that God’s "strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). A slogan that tells a girl to look inward for power will fail her on her worst day, because the well runs dry. A father can tell his daughter: you are not weak, and you were not made to be a decoration — but your strength is borrowed, and the Lender is faithful. Be a Deborah, not a brand.

Webster 1828 Definition

Riot grrrl rallying cry (c. 1991) taken worldwide by the Spice Girls (1996–97) for female confidence and independence; Scripture honors strong women like Deborah and the virtuous wife but says power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11).

expand to see more

GIRL POWER, n. (Gen X slang, early 1990s riot grrrl; mainstream 1996–97 via the Spice Girls) Female confidence, solidarity, and independence, as a slogan or cheer. "Girl power!"

Roots in the Olympia, Washington, punk scene (Bikini Kill and its zines, c. 1991); spelled grrrl in the underground.

Mainstreamed as merchandise in the "Wannabe" years: T-shirts, lunchboxes, dolls; later a staple of advertising.

Webster 1828: POWER, n. [The Latin has posse, possum, potes, potentia. The primary sense of the verb is to strain, to exert force.] 1. In a philosophical sense, the faculty of doing or performing any thing; the faculty of moving or of producing a change in something; ability or strength. …

Decode for parents: the slogan answers a daughter’s real question about strength; Scripture answers it better — strength from God, spent in His service.

Key Scripture

Psa 62:11 — "God hath spoken once; twice have I heard this; that power belongeth unto God."

Pro 31:17 — "She girdeth her loins with strength, and strengtheneth her arms."

Pro 31:25 — "Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come."

Jdg 5:7 — "The inhabitants of the villages ceased, they ceased in Israel, until that I Deborah arose, that I arose a mother in Israel."

2Co 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Modern Corruption

Girl power tells a daughter that strength is hers to summon from within; Scripture clothes a woman in strength and honour but locates all power in God, made perfect in weakness.

expand to see more

Power from within. The slogan’s premise is that a girl’s strength is already inside her, waiting to be believed in. It sells well and wears thin. Every girl meets the day when confidence runs out — a loss, a sin, a betrayal — and a creed of self-power has nothing to say to her then. The Psalmist heard God speak twice on the matter: "power belongeth unto God" (Psa 62:11). Paul learned it in his own weakness: "my strength is made perfect in weakness" (2Co 12:9). That is a word for daughters and sons alike.

The strong women of Scripture. The church has no reason to answer the slogan with a shrug, as if godly women were meant to be feeble. Deborah judged Israel and arose a mother in Israel (Jdg 5:7); the virtuous woman girds her loins with strength (Pro 31:17) and wears strength and honour as her clothing (Pro 31:25). Their strength served God, their households, and their people, not a brand. A daughter who learns that will be stronger than any slogan, and freer than any lunchbox promised.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin posse → Old French poer → English power; riot grrrl girl power (Olympia, c. 1991) → Spice Girls (1996–97) → slogan and merchandise; Scripture: power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11).

Latin posse — to be able; Old French poer → English power

c. 1991: riot grrrl punk scene, Olympia and Washington, D.C.; Bikini Kill

1996–97: the Spice Girls make girl power a worldwide pop slogan

Late 1990s: T-shirts, lunchboxes, advertising copy

Scripture’s strong women: Deborah (Jdg 5:7), the virtuous woman (Pro 31:25); the source: God (Psa 62:11)

Usage

""Girl power!" — printed on a 1997 lunchbox."

"Strength and honour are her clothing (Pro 31:25) — strength worn, not manufactured."

"Power belongeth unto God (Psa 62:11), and He perfects it in weakness (2Co 12:9)."
